problems.form_value: 293 writers were randomly assigned to write an eight-sentence story with no AI (Human-only), with the option to request one three-sentence GPT-4 story idea, or with the option to request up to five such ideas.
problems.source_says: 293 is the number analyzed after exclusions, not the number randomized. The three Human-only writers dropped for admitting AI use had already been assigned, so at least 296 people were randomized (at least 297 given the second problem below). The paper never prints the randomized total. The Introduction (p. 1) loosely calls the 293 'recruited', but Methods (p. 7) show the drops came after assignment. The form's own participants block correctly leaves n_randomized null, so the summary contradicts it. Correct wording: 'Writers were randomly assigned ... and 293 were analyzed.'
problems.quote: Three participants in the Human-only condition admitted to using generative AI during their story writing exercise and—as per our preregistration—were therefore dropped from the analysis, resulting in a total number of writers and stories of 293.
problems.locator: p. 7, Materials and Methods, 'Writer study and experimental conditions', first paragraph

problems.form_value: participants.exclusions: 'the paper does not say whether the 13 dropouts left before or after assignment, so the number randomized is not stated'. open_questions[0]: 'it is unclear whether the 13 writers who dropped out before completing had been assigned.'
problems.source_says: The paper shows that some of the 13 non-completers had been assigned and had written a story: evaluations of stories by writers who did not complete the writer study existed and were dropped. Only the 13 can be such writers, because the other 191 never consented. The p. 8 counts agree: 600 evaluators were each shown 6 stories (3600 evaluations), 3519 remain, so 81 were dropped (5 x 2 + 71 x 1). Retained stories drew 9 to 14 evaluations each, so 81 dropped evaluations cover roughly 6 to 9 stories, more than the 3 AI-admitting writers' stories. Attrition after randomization is therefore at least 4 people, and the randomized total lies between 297 and 309 (the 309 who consented). n_randomized = null stays correct. Only the narrative is incomplete.
problems.quote: The evaluations associated with the writers who did not complete the writer study and those in the Human-only condition who acknowledged using AI to complete the story were dropped.
problems.locator: p. 7, Materials and Methods, 'Evaluator study', first paragraph, last sentence; evaluation counts on p. 8, 'Evaluator study', paragraph beginning 'There were a total of 3519 evaluations'

confirmed: S1 analyzed 293 writers, and they are people: each writer wrote one story, so 293 writers give 293 stories (p. 7, 'Writer study and experimental conditions', first paragraph; p. 1, right column, last paragraph: 'N = 293 participants ("writers")'; p. 8, 'Statistical analysis': 'each writer produces one story').

Attrition adds up: 500 began, minus 169 who exited before consent, 22 dropped for not consenting, 13 who dropped out before completing, and 3 Human-only writers who admitted AI use, leaves 293 (p. 7, 'Writer study and experimental conditions', first paragraph).

Assignment came after consent and the DAT, and the paper prints no randomized total, overall or by arm. Fig. 1 shows only '293 writer stories'. n_randomized = null for S1 and for all three arms is right (p. 2, Fig. 1 and caption; p. 7, 'Writer study and experimental conditions').

Analyzed arm counts are 100 (one GenAI idea) and 98 (five GenAI ideas). They are analysis-sample counts: (82 + 93)/198 = 88.4 percent and 24/98 = 24.5 percent reproduce the printed shares (p. 2, Results, 'Baseline versus generative AI conditions', second paragraph).

The Human-only analyzed count is printed nowhere in the text or in Figs. 1 to 4. Subtraction gives 95 (293 - 100 - 98). The form's null, with 95 noted in open_questions, is defensible (pp. 1-9; Figs. 1-4 on pp. 2-5).
All three AI-use exclusions came from the Human-only arm, so they do not change the AI-arm counts (p. 7, 'Writer study and experimental conditions', first paragraph).

The 600 evaluators are a separate sample who had not taken part in the writer study. They rated stories and were not assigned to AI, so the form keeps them out of the people count (p. 2, left column, 'In the second phase'; p. 7, 'Evaluator study', first paragraph).

Evaluation counts add up: 5 x 4 + 71 x 5 + 524 x 6 = 3519 evaluations from 5 + 71 + 524 = 600 evaluators, and the per-story distribution sums to 293 stories and 3519 evaluations. The form records 3519 as n_units with unit 'rating', not as people (p. 8, 'Evaluator study', paragraph beginning 'There were a total of 3519 evaluations').
The DAT score exists for 291 of 293 writers. This limits only the DAT heterogeneity analyses (p. 3, 'Heterogeneity by inherent creativity', first paragraph).

The paper has one writer experiment, coded as the single study S1, and no person appears twice within it: evaluators 'had not previously participated in the writer study' (p. 7, 'Evaluator study', first paragraph).

No other screened paper shares these writers. candidates.json holds no other version of c006 (other_versions is empty). c023 is a review that only cites the paper, and c004 is a theory paper (forms/c023.json; forms/c004.json). c128 (Wan and Kalman, arXiv 2504.13868) extends the design with a new sample: '100 participants were recruited on Prolific, using the same recruitment criteria and protocol used by [1]' (arXiv 2504.13868v1 HTML, methods, read by web fetch; no local PDF).
At least 50 people: S1 alone analyzed 293 writers, and each arm has at least 95 (p. 7; p. 2).

The participants quote is verbatim, and the who, population, and country fields match the text: Prolific, UK-based, approval rating of at least 95 percent from 100 to 1,000,000 prior submissions, not selected on writing skill or creativity (p. 7, 'Writer study and experimental conditions', first paragraph).
summary: The people counts in S1 hold: 293 writers were analyzed (one story each), 100 and 98 of them in the two AI arms, and the 50-person criterion is met with no sample shared with another paper. The conclusion is still refuted on two narrative points: paper_design_summary calls the 293 analyzed writers 'randomly assigned' although at least 296 were assigned, and the attrition note says the timing of the 13 dropouts is unknown although p. 7 shows that some of them had been assigned and had written stories.
